Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Name early that everyone feels a little awkward, you included. Never assume anyone is or isn’t sexually active. Questions can go to a counselor privately; if something comes up that happened to a student, walk them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Students arrive with very different family and faith rules about sex, different identities, and some have already had sex, wanted or not; keep every example open to any couple and never assume who is waiting or why.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can sort where they learn about sex by how much to trust it, spot common myths, explain why porn is a staged show and what it leaves out, check any situation against FRIES, name the basics of STIs and safer sex, and know where to take a question.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minFour ground rules
  2. 5 minWhere people our age learn about sex: turn and talk, share out
  3. 6 minMyth or reality, one per slide
  4. 3 minThree of four teens have seen porn
  5. 7 minPorn is pro wrestling, and what a camera cuts out
  6. 6 minConsent is FRIES
  7. 5 minSTIs and safer sex, and am I ready? (just for you)
  8. 10 minEvery student, where else this shows up, where to go with questions

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Ground rules, myth or reality, porn is pro wrestling, FRIES, am I ready, and where to go with questions.

Before you teach
Assume someone in the room has lived this.

Someone may have been pressured, touched without asking, or shown porn by an older kid or an adult. Say at the start that nobody shares their own story and anyone can step out. When you reach "a body reacting isn't a yes," say it slowly. For a survivor, that line can lift years of confusion.

Keep it shame-free.

Seeing porn doesn't make anyone gross, and neither does curiosity. Shame shuts the room down. This line works: "Having seen porn doesn't make you a bad person. Questioning what it teaches makes you a smart one."

Waiting and not waiting both get respect.

"Not yet" is a strong answer for most 9th graders, and the lesson says so. Some students have already had sex. Don't let the waiting message turn into a judgment of them. Anyone can decide "not again for now."

Be plain about rough sex and choking.

If it comes up, answer it straight and once: pressure on the neck can cut off blood to the brain within seconds, and there's no safe way to do it. Doing it without asking is never okay, and students can tell someone.

Read every card before you answer.

Ninth graders ask more on a card than out loud. Skip any that name a real person. If a card worries you, take it to a counselor. If you don't know an answer, say you'll find out, and do.

Stay inside your school's rules.

Some schools set limits on contraception talk or demonstrations. Stick to the facts on the slides and send detailed questions to the nurse or a doctor.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Faith and family values.

Some students come from families or faiths where sex waits for marriage, or where it's never talked about. Waiting is presented as a respected choice, not a lecture. Point to a parent, older cousin, faith leader, doctor or counselor as people a student might ask, and let each student pick who fits.

LGBTQ+ students.

Every example in the deck works for any couple. Keep it that way if you add your own. STI facts apply to everyone, including oral and anal sex, and the pill line is about pregnancy only. Some LGBTQ+ students first saw people like them in porn; say that makes sense, and that real relationships take the same trust and talking.

Every gender.

"Guys always want sex" is on the myth list on purpose. Guys get pressured too and are less likely to say so. Don't assign roles by gender in the FRIES round; the names are mixed on purpose.

Students who don't want sex at all.

Some students aren't interested, now or ever, and that's a real and normal way to be. "Not yet" and "not for me" are both full answers.

Race and bodies.

Porn sells stereotypes about race and about bodies. Over half of teens who'd seen porn saw Black people shown in stereotyped ways. If you discuss "bodies are supposed to look like that," say plainly that the screen is a casting call, and that includes skin color, size and disability.

Disability and neurodivergence.

Students who read social cues differently benefit from the clear words in FRIES: a real yes, out loud, and anyone can stop. A disability never takes away someone's right to say yes or no, or to learn this.

What the research says

About 1 in 3 U.S. high school students has ever had sex. In 9th grade the share is much lower.

CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2023

73% of teens 13 to 17 had seen porn online; the average age they first saw it was 12, and more had seen it by accident than on purpose. Over half of those who'd seen it had seen violent or aggressive porn.

Robb and Mann, Teens and Pornography, Common Sense Media, 2023

More teens said they'd learned a lot about sex from a trusted adult (47%) than from porn (27%). Only 33% of teens who'd seen porn had ever seen anyone in it ask for consent.

Robb and Mann, Common Sense Media, 2023

In 304 scenes from best-selling porn videos, 88% included physical aggression, and the person on the receiving end was shown enjoying it or not reacting 95% of the time.

Bridges et al., Violence Against Women, 2010

People ages 15 to 24 account for about half of new STIs in the U.S. each year, and many infections have no symptoms.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, STI surveillance

FRIES (freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, specific) is Planned Parenthood's framework. It maps onto the four checks in Consent, Clearly.

Planned Parenthood, "What is sexual consent?"
